outcome: Nothing settles Dubner's conjecture since 26 January 2024. The only post-window work on this statement itself is arXiv:2608.02381 (Tushar Pandey, v1 3 Aug 2026, v2 26 Aug 2026), which reruns the both-twin exception check to 10^11 and finds only the known exceptions, none above 4208, while stating that the conjecture is not verified above 10^11 by these computations; its new theorem and its 10^14 verification concern a weaker statement, (S), prime plus twin member.
problem_asks: The statement: every even number n greater than 4208 is the sum of two primes, each of which has a twin (a prime p has a twin when p-2 or p+2 is also prime). Parts: (a) for every even n > 4208 there exist primes p and q with n = p + q; (b) p has a twin; (c) q has a twin. Equivalently, the set of even n with no such decomposition is finite and lies in [0, 4208]; the known exceptions are the 35 even numbers in OEIS A007534 (2, 4, 94, 96, 98, 400, 402, 404, 514, 516, 518, 784, 786, 788, 904, 906, 908, 1114, 1116, 1118, 1144, 1146, 1148, 1264, 1266, 1268, 1354, 1356, 1358, 3244, 3246, 3248, 4204, 4206, 4208). Not asked by this bullet: Goldbach's conjecture for all even n > 2 (which the statement would imply for n > 4208), the twin prime conjecture (which it would imply), counts or densities of such decompositions, and the threshold 4208 as a separate question.

events.what_happened: Harvey Dubner (1928-2019) is credited with the conjecture. Rosetta Code dates the proposal to 2000 and gives the first name as Henry ('In 2000, Henry Dubner proposed a stronger conjecture'). OEIS A007534 cites Dubner, 'Twin Prime Conjectures', Journal of Recreational Mathematics 30(3), 1999-2000; I did not locate that item. Pandey's 2026 paper (arXiv:2608.02381) says Dubner's own direct search covered multiples of 6 up to 2x10^10 and found the eleven exceptional centres and no others; I did not find the date or publication of that search.
events.delivers: The statement only, with the exceptions below 4208 listed as 33 even numbers in [6, 4208]. Dubner's own computational search to 2x10^10 is reported by others (undated; the date is not established). No proof is claimed in any source I read.
events.remains: Everything: the statement for all even n > 4208.
events.time_since_posted: about 26 years if the proposal is dated 2000
events.directly_checkable: The exceptions below 4208 can be checked by hand for each n (see the n = 94 example under arXiv:2608.02381).
events.doubts: Sources disagree on the first name (Harvey in Wikipedia, Henry in Rosetta Code) and on the year (2000 in Rosetta Code; the JRM volume is 1999-2000). The JRM item was not located, so the 2000 date and the 2x10^10 search are unconfirmed.
events.direction: The statement itself; it asserts that the exceptional set is finite and contained in [0, 4208].

events.what_happened: Dan Zwillinger, 'A Goldbach conjecture using twin primes', Mathematics of Computation 33(147), 1979, p. 1071 (MathSciNet review MR 528060). Per the AMS catalogue record (the AMS page returned 403 to my fetch; the record was read from a search summary), a computer check of even numbers up to 10^6 found 33 exceptions to the sum-of-two-twin-primes representation, all below 5000; the largest even number up to 500,000 with only one such representation is 24098. OEIS A266948 cites the paper.
events.delivers: A finite computation: no exceptions above 5000 up to 10^6 (the exceptional set in that range is the known list). Restricted to n <= 10^6; per section 2.1 this is finitely many instances of the universal claim.
events.remains: The statement for all even n > 10^6.

checked_by.what_they_did: Published a review of the 1979 paper (per AMS catalogue).

events.directly_checkable: Computational; not checkable by hand beyond small n.
events.doubts: The paper itself was not read. Figures come from the AMS catalogue summary and the OEIS A266948 comment. Note that the AMS summary says 'a computer check of even numbers up to one million', which I have taken at face value.
events.direction: Consistent with the statement; no counterexample in the range checked.

events.what_happened: Andrei Allakhverdov, 'Some problems in additive number theory', arXiv:1402.6571 (math.GM). The abstract (read) presents a double-sieve method for additive problems with primes and says it is applied to the 'Goldbach-Euler conjecture and the twin primes conjecture' and that the method 'does not use empirical and heuristic reasoning'. A search summary of the PDF (body not readable by my fetch) reports a section 4.2 'The strengthened Goldbach-Euler conjecture', a Proposition 13 asking how many even numbers are sums of two primes each having a twin, and a numerical check of 30,000 triples of even numbers in which 12 lacked such a representation; it also says the paper takes the Goldbach-Euler and twin prime conjectures as given.
events.revisions: v1 20 Feb 2014; v2 20 Apr 2014; v3 7 Jan 2017 (current).
events.delivers: Per the abstract: a sieve method for additive problems. Per the search summary (unverified by me): a conditional proposition for a strengthened Goldbach-Euler statement, in which both summands have twins, supported by a numerical check. Whether this statement is the same as Dubner's, including the threshold 4208, is not established from what I could read.
events.remains: The statement for all even n above 4208, unless the proposition is unconditional, which the summary does not say.
events.directly_checkable: The 30,000-triple check could be reproduced in principle; I could not read the method or the list.
events.doubts: The abstract says the method uses no empirical or heuristic reasoning, while the search summary reports a numerical check and conditional use of the conjectures. These readings are in tension and I could not resolve them without the body text. Posted to math.GM; no peer review or expert reading found.
events.direction: If the summary is right: a conditional proposition for a Dubner-type statement plus numerical evidence; no counterexample. Cuts toward the statement, if at all.

events.what_happened: Frank Vega, preprints.org manuscript 202002.0379 (the identifier implies a February 2020 posting). The preprints.org pages returned 403 to my fetch, so the content is from a search summary only: the summary quotes 'We prove there are infinite even numbers that comply the Dubner's conjecture, where this also implies that the Twin prime conjecture is true'.
events.revisions: Multiple versions in the download URL (v3 cited); version history not read.
events.delivers: Claimed: infinitely many even numbers are sums of two twin members (the both-twin form of Dubner's statement), and this is said to imply the twin prime conjecture. The inference is valid for the both-twin form: if infinitely many even numbers are such sums, the set of twin members is infinite, because a finite set T would give only finitely many sums in T + T. The claim's content is therefore the infinitude, which is not established by anything I could read.
events.remains: The statement for all even n > 4208, and the claimed infinitude is not verified.
events.directly_checkable: No: the claim is an argument, not an object.
events.doubts: Not read. The same author's EasyChair preprint 3388 claims a proof of the twin prime conjecture by complexity theory (next event), with no independent check found. No expert reading found.
events.direction: Claims infinitely many even numbers satisfy the both-twin statement, and therefore infinitely many twin primes. Unverified.

events.what_happened: Frank Vega, 'The Complexity of the Twin Prime Conjecture', EasyChair Preprint 3388, dated 12 May 2020 (page opened). It claims 'We prove the Twin prime conjecture using the Complexity Theory', resting on a claimed equivalence between unary and binary versions of languages in nondeterministic space classes. The page I opened does not mention Dubner's conjecture. A search summary of the same EasyChair entry says it does mention Dubner's conjecture and argues that infinitely many even numbers comply. I could not reconcile the two.
events.revisions: One entry on the page; no revisions shown.
events.delivers: Claimed: the twin prime conjecture (infinitely many twin primes). As far as the page I opened shows, not a statement about Dubner's conjecture.
events.remains: Dubner's statement, and, if the claim fails, the twin prime conjecture itself.
events.directly_checkable: No: the argument is abstract and the proof is not visible in the abstract I read.
events.doubts: EasyChair preprint, not peer reviewed, with no verification on the page. The argument's link to prime gaps is not visible in what I read. Conflict between the page and the search summary on whether Dubner's conjecture is discussed.
events.direction: Claims a proof of the twin prime conjecture. Unverified. Neighbouring problem on the page I read.

events.what_happened: Harvey Dubner, 'Twin Prime Statistics', Journal of Integer Sequences 8 (2005), Article 05.4.2 (received 3 May 2005; published 29 Aug 2005; page opened). Gives statistical support for the Hardy-Littlewood twin prime count up to 10^600. The page does not mention Dubner's conjecture about even numbers above 4208. Discarded: it is about a different conjecture.
events.delivers: Statistical evidence for the Hardy-Littlewood count of twin primes (a neighbouring conjecture). Nothing about sums of two twin primes.
events.direction: Neighbouring problem. Cuts neither way on Dubner's statement.

events.what_happened: Comment on OEIS A007534 by Tushar Pandey, dated 28 Jul 2026: 'No other k < 10^11.' This is six days before the arXiv posting of the same computation (next event). The OEIS page also now cites arXiv:2608.02381 in its references.
events.delivers: A finite computation: no both-twin exceptions to the statement beyond the 35-term list for k < 10^11. Restricted to k < 10^11.
events.doubts: A single author's claim in an OEIS comment, with no code cited on the page. The later arXiv paper is the fuller account.
events.direction: Consistent with the statement; no exception above 4208 found up to 10^11.

events.what_happened: Tushar Pandey, 'An intermediate conjecture between Goldbach and Dubner: every even number is the sum of a prime and a twin prime', arXiv:2608.02381 (math.NT; single author, no affiliation on the arXiv page). Read: the arXiv abstract page and an HTML rendering of v2, summarised by WebFetch (the PDF is binary to my fetch). The paper defines a twin member as a prime t with t-2 or t+2 prime, and states Dubner's conjecture as: every even n > 4208 is a sum of two twin members. It also states an intermediate conjecture (S): every even n >= 6 is p + t with p prime and t a twin member. It claims (S) is verified for every even n with 6 <= n <= 10^14, using the authors' C kernel on 16 threads (about 9.0 hours on a laptop) with cross-checks to 10^12 and 10^13 (the 10^13 prefix agrees with an earlier run, and Tomas Oliveira e Silva independently verified (S) to 10^13 per the acknowledgements). For Dubner's statement itself, the both-twin run reaches 10^11, re-derives the 33 known exceptions in [6, 4208] (in 11 triples centred at 6m for m in {16, 67, 86, 131, 151, 186, 191, 211, 226, 541, 701}, e.g. 6 x 701 = 4206), and finds no others; the paper states that Dubner's conjecture is not verified above 10^11 by these computations. Main theorem: under a hypothesis TW(c) (twin primes up to z number at least c z / log^2 z for z >= z0), the even numbers representable as p + t have lower density at least c/K for an absolute K; the paper notes that positive density would itself imply the twin prime conjecture, so the theorem cannot be unconditional. v1 posted 3 Aug 2026 (per search summary, its run covered 10^11); v2 26 Aug 2026 extended (S) to 10^14 and added the conditional density theorem.
events.revisions: v1 3 Aug 2026 (both-twin run to 10^11 per search summary); v2 26 Aug 2026 (verification of (S) extended to 10^14; conditional Romanov-type density theorem added; references updated). Companion Zenodo software record 'pandey-tushar/twin-goldbach-note' v1.4, 26 Aug 2026, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22117179 (MIT licence); the arXiv comment's DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21744861 resolves to that same v1.4 record. I did not reconcile the two DOIs.
events.delivers: For Dubner's statement: computation (the authors' both-twin run) that the even numbers in (4208, 10^11] are all sums of two twin members, so the only exceptions up to 10^11 are the 33 known ones in [6, 4208]. Restrictions: computational only, to 10^11, in a single run by the authors (with Dubner's own earlier search to 2x10^10 cited by them). For (S), which is not Dubner's statement: verified for every even 6 <= n <= 10^14 (single run per the paper, cross-checked to 10^13 by Oliveira e Silva); a conditional lower-density theorem under TW(c). The density theorem is conditional on TW(c); the paper also states that positive density of prime-plus-twin representations would itself imply the twin prime conjecture, so the theorem is not a route to Dubner's statement.
events.remains: Dubner's statement for every even n > 10^11 (the paper says it is not verified above 10^11 by these computations). The (S) statement for all n, and the TW(c) hypothesis, are not Dubner's question and are not established. Goldbach and the twin prime conjecture are implied by Dubner's statement and are not settled by this event.

checked_by.qualification: Author of the published even-Goldbach verification to 4x10^18 (Oliveira e Silva, Herzog, Pardi, Math. Comp. 2014); computational number theorist
checked_by.what_they_did: Per the paper's acknowledgements, independently verified (S) to 10^13 with a program sharing no code with the authors'. No public statement by him found; the report comes from the author's own acknowledgement. The check is of (S), not of Dubner's statement.
checked_by.where: https://arxiv.org/html/2608.02381v2 (acknowledgements, read via a summary of the HTML rendering)

events.directly_checkable: Computational: the authors archive code and per-block data on Zenodo. Individual exceptions can be checked by hand. For n = 94, the twin members t up to 47 are 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19, 29, 31, 41, 43; the values 94 - t (91, 89, 87, 83, 81, 77, 75, 65, 63, 53, 51) include no twin member (89, 83, 53 are prime but have no prime at distance 2), so 94 is an exception. The witness for the largest least Dubner witness (n = 35,984,652,098, least twin t = 414,769) is checkable only by primality testing of numbers near 3.6 x 10^10.
events.doubts: (1) Single author with no affiliation; I found no journal submission and no expert written reading as of 10 Oct 2026. (2) Scope changed between versions: v2 extended (S) from 10^11 to 10^14 and added a conditional density theorem. The 10^14 result is a single run of the authors' kernel per the paper, and the 10^12 check is also a single pass. (3) The paper states that Dubner's statement is not verified above 10^11, so the claim does not reach the statement's full range. (4) The Sahu IRJET 2024 paper, which the Zenodo note cites as the earliest formulation of (S), could not be found. (5) The DOI discrepancy noted above. (6) The full PDF was not readable to me, so the figures come from a summary of the HTML rendering and the abstract page.
events.direction: For Dubner's statement: consistent with it up to 10^11, with no counterexample and no new exception. The paper does not prove or disprove the statement; its new theorem concerns (S) and is conditional. Neither result is a counterexample.
events.object: No counterexample. Two explicit computational objects: (i) the list of the 33 exceptions in [6, 4208] reproduced by the both-twin run, arranged as 11 consecutive-even triples centred at 6m for m in {16, 67, 86, 131, 151, 186, 191, 211, 226, 541, 701}; (ii) the largest least Dubner witness found: n = 35,984,652,098 written as t + (n - t) with both t and n - t twin members, least such t = 414,769. The witness is an explicit representation, consistent with the conjecture. Separately for (S), not Dubner's statement: the least twin witness at n = 31,819,171,719,758 is 23,029, the largest in the 10^14 run.
people: Tomas Oliveira e Silva (independent check of (S) to 10^13, per the acknowledgements)

disputes.summary: Dubner's first name is Harvey in Wikipedia and Henry in Rosetta Code; the proposal year is given as 2000 in Rosetta Code, while the cited JRM item is 1999-2000 and was not located.

Counts of exceptions are given as 33 (in [6, 4208], arXiv:2608.02381 and Zwillinger), 34 (below 4208, a Scribd summary) and 35 (all, including 2, 4 and 4208, OEIS A007534, ProofWiki, MathWorks). These differ only in conventions; the lists agree.
The EasyChair 3388 page by Frank Vega does not mention Dubner's conjecture on the page I opened, while a search summary says it does. Unresolved.

summary: Dubner's conjecture (every even n > 4208 is a sum of two primes each having a twin) has no article of its own. Wikipedia's bullet links only to 'prime number' and 'twin prime'; the statement appears in the Harvey Dubner article, which I opened. That sentence carries no citation tag, although one search summary said it did. Nothing I found proves or disproves the statement. The only post-window work on the statement itself is arXiv:2608.02381 (Tushar Pandey, v1 3 Aug 2026, v2 26 Aug 2026), read from the abstract page and an HTML rendering because the PDF was unreadable. Its both-twin run reproduces the 33 known exceptions in [6, 4208] for every even n up to 10^11 and finds no others, and the paper says the statement is not verified above 10^11 by these computations. The paper's new theorem and its 10^14 verification concern a weaker statement, (S): every even n >= 6 is a prime plus a twin member; the density theorem is conditional on a twin-prime lower bound. The exception list is consistent across OEIS, ProofWiki, the arXiv paper and Zwillinger's 1979 computation to 10^6; the eleven triple-centres 6m match the list (for example 6 x 701 = 4206). The OEIS A007534 comment by the same author (28 Jul 2026, 'No other k < 10^11') predates the arXiv posting, and T. D. Noe's 2007 OEIS comment ('No other k < 10^9') is the earliest dated OEIS verification; Zwillinger's 1979 computation to 10^6 is earlier still. Close call: whether a finite check of the exceptional set to 10^11 moves the problem. The exceptional set is the conjecture's own quantity, and the run certifies it further than Dubner's earlier search to 2x10^10, which is the reading that moves it; but the statement is universal over n > 4208, so each extra range is finitely many instances, which is the Collatz reading that moves nothing. I record the event and leave the call to the judging pass. Older items: Allakhverdov's 2014 arXiv paper (abstract says the method uses no empirical reasoning; a search summary of its body reports a Proposition 13 with a 30,000-triple numerical check, and I could not read the body); Vega's 2020 claims on preprints.org and EasyChair, which assert the twin prime conjecture and, for preprints.org, a Dubner-implication whose inference is valid for the both-twin form but whose infinitude claim I could not check; and Dubner's 2005 JIS paper, which concerns the Hardy-Littlewood count and is discarded. AI: no source I read names an AI system for Dubner's statement or for arXiv:2608.02381, whose abstract, comments, Zenodo description and HTML rendering mention none. The formal-conjectures issue #3628 says it was 'generated by an AI agent and reviewed by' its author; the agent is unnamed, so ai.systems is empty and none_found is false for that event. Two neighbouring twin-prime results carry AI attribution but bear on bounded gaps, not on this statement: OpenAI's 186 preprint (credited to 'GPT-6 Astra' by press and a tracker, whose PDF I could not read; its README names no AI) and Axiom's BGP246 Lean formalisation, which AxiomProver is said to have produced and which formalises existing human proofs. Neither is recorded in ai.systems because I have no authors' own sentence for either. The Goldbach-Liouville 'GPT-6 Astra' result is a Goldbach analogue and belongs in the Goldbach record. Searches for the Dubner statement with AI terms found no AI involvement.
competing_reading: Read strictly, the only post-window item is a finite computation of a universal statement, which by section 2.1 moves nothing: the statement says the exceptions are finite and contained in [0, 4208], and Collatz shows that verification to any bound counts for nothing. On that reading, nothing has happened to the problem since January 2024, and arXiv:2608.02381's Dubner part is one more instance. Read the other way, the statement names the exceptional set as its own quantity (as with abc in section 2.1), and the August 2026 run is a certified, reproducible census of that set to 10^11, five times further than Dubner's earlier search; on that reading the event moves a quantity the statement names, though not to the end of the statement's range. The Vega preprints, if read as the summary reports, would move the infinitude of both-twin representations, but nothing I read supports that claim, so it does not change the status.
what_would_settle_it: (1) For the scope call: whether the 10^11 run changes what the statement asserts, which needs the arXiv PDF body (the both-twin section and its stated limit) and Dubner's own 2x10^10 search, which I could not date. (2) For the doubts: an expert reading of arXiv:2608.02381 or a journal submission; the v1 and v2 texts side by side to confirm the 10^11 claim was in v1; Zenodo's data, to reconcile the two DOIs. (3) For the older events: the Allakhverdov Section 4.2 and Proposition 13 text; the preprints.org 202002.0379 text; the EasyChair 3388 PDF to settle whether Dubner's conjecture is discussed; the 1979 Zwillinger paper itself. (4) For AI: the OpenAI PDF's own sentence on how GPT-6 Astra was used, if the bounded-gap result is to be attributed; the formal-conjectures Dubner.lean file, if the agent's role in the formal statement matters for later passes.

judgement.why: The statement is universal over all even n > 4208. Every computational event (Zwillinger to 10^6, Noe to 10^9, Pandey to 10^11 in both the OEIS comment and the arXiv paper) checks finitely many instances, so each is scored instances (F5). The researcher's alternative reading, that the exceptional set is a quantity the statement names, does not hold: the statement asserts the set is contained in [0, 4208], and no finite census moves that assertion. Pandey's theorem and its 10^14 run concern the weaker statement (S), and the theorem is conditional, so neither adds anything beyond instances. Pandey's least-witness representation is just one instance, not an object bearing on the statement. Dubner's proposal is the statement itself, so it is none. The formal-conjectures entry formalises the statement only, so it is none. Its unnamed AI agent drafted the issue text and did no mathematics, so its AI role is none. Vega's claims target the twin prime conjecture or an infinitude variant, and they carry several F10 signals together, so they are not_credible as well as variant. Dubner 2005 and the two bounded-gap results are neighbouring problems, so variant. Their AI attributions are irrelevant here and have no authors' quote behind them.
judgement.doubts: Zwillinger's 'digested' rests on publication in Math. Comp. per a catalogue summary. It is immaterial, because the event is discarded as instances.
